title: No mocking, no nicknames
hook: don't mock others, they may be better than you, and don't insult with names (49:11)

segments.voice: Yesterday, make peace between them: islah, mending, the work the verse gives to bystanders. Your line was repair with fairness, so the thing can hold. Whose kind word did you carry? Day five hundred eighty-six.
screen: `REPAIR WITH FAIRNESS, SO THE THING CAN HOLD.`

segments.voice: Almost everyone had one. The nickname from middle school that started as a joke about your ears, your name, your accent, your weight, and followed you for years. Some people laugh about theirs now. Some still flinch when they hear it. The people who gave them out mostly forgot within a week. Surah Al-Hujurat, the surah of how a community talks, spends a whole verse on this, and the reason it gives is not the one you'd expect.

Verse eleven, in Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! Let not a folk deride a folk who may be better than they (are), nor let women (deride) women who may be better than they are; neither defame one another, nor insult one another by nicknames." Three things are named. Mocking, sakhar: laughing at someone to make them small. Defaming, lamz: the little digs, the jab disguised as a joke. And insulting with nicknames, tanabuz bil-alqab: the label that sticks. And look at the reason the verse gives. Not that mocking is rude. That the one you mock may be better than you. You can see a person's ears or accent. You can't see their standing with God. The mockery assumes a ranking the mocker has no access to. A report in Sunan Abi Dawud gives the setting. A man from the Banu Salamah said the verse came down about them. When the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Medina, many men had two or three names, and when he called someone by one of them, people would say: Messenger of God, that one makes him angry. So the verse was revealed. Notice the detail: the Prophet himself didn't know which names stung. Nicknames aren't always cruel. Many Companions carried names they loved: Abu Hurayrah, father of the little cat. The line the scholars draw is the one the verse draws: whether the name is one the person dislikes. A hadith in Sahih Muslim sums it up: it is evil enough for a person to look down on his brother.
screen: `MOCKING, DIGS, AND LABELS THAT STICK.` · `THEY MAY BE BETTER THAN YOU.` · `NAMES THAT MADE SOMEONE ANGRY.` · `ABU HURAYRAH LOVED HIS.`

segments.voice: The practice: stop one nickname. Sit, and breathe. Think of the names you use for people, out loud or in your head: a coworker, a sibling, a politician, a driver who cut you off. Find one that's really a small insult. Picture that person hearing it. Then decide to drop it, starting today, and choose their real name instead. If you were given a name that still stings, you can also let yourself set it down. If you pray, you can pray for them. The bell holds the time.
No mocking. The rule of 49:11: no deriding, no digs, no hurtful nicknames, because the one you mock may be better than you. Today's word.
Your line: they may be better. Today, when you're tempted to laugh at someone, remind yourself you can't see their whole story, and say their real name. Day five hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Muslim scholars count mocking and hurtful nicknames among the sins of the tongue; affectionate names a person welcomes, like Abu Hurayrah, are accepted, while names someone dislikes are avoided.

myth: scholars draw the line at names the person dislikes; Abu Hurayrah loved his.
the verse's reason is that the one mocked may be better
you can't see someone's standing with God.
the verse names women as well as men
it says neither men nor women should deride one another.

fork.setup: the Prophet arrives in Medina and calls a man by one of his names. people say it makes him angry. what follows, in the report?
options: the verse against hurtful nicknames comes down.
fork.reveal: a man of Banu Salamah said 49:11 was revealed about this, in Sunan Abi Dawud.

original.note: Arabic: and do not insult one another with nicknames (49:11).

trapdoor: what you thought: teasing is harmless.
what it means: mocking, digs and hurtful labels assume a ranking you can't see; the one mocked may be better.
what a scholar hears: three distinct sins, sakhar, lamz and tanabuz; Abu Dawud's report of Banu Salamah gives the occasion.
